title: Christianity in Africa and Nigeria
summary: The story of the gospel in Africa from the New Testament to today, with a focus on Nigeria: early churches, missions, African-led churches, growth, and the challenges and calling of the African church.
description: Africa has a long and rich Christian history. This course traces Christianity on the continent from the Ethiopian official and the North African fathers, through the ancient Ethiopian church and early Catholic contacts, to the nineteenth-century missions in Nigeria and the rise of African-initiated churches. It then examines the growth of the Nigerian church, its theology and mission, and the challenges it faces: syncretism, prosperity teaching, persecution and discipleship.
objectives: Trace Christianity in Africa from the first century to today
Describe how the gospel came to different parts of Nigeria
Explain the rise and character of African-initiated churches
Engage key African Christian thinkers and missions
Analyse the challenges and calling of the Nigerian church today
outcomes: Show the ancient roots of African Christianity
Describe the work of Crowther, Slessor, SIM and others in Nigeria
Explain the significance of African-initiated churches
Describe the contribution of Byang Kato and Nigerian mission agencies
Respond biblically to syncretism and other challenges

modules.title: Ancient African Christianity
modules.intro: Christianity in Africa is ancient. This week we survey the first fifteen centuries.

lessons.title: Africa in the biblical story
lessons.body:
Africa appears throughout Scripture. Egypt sheltered Abraham, Joseph, Israel and the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:13-15). Moses married a Cushite woman (Numbers 12:1). Ebed-melech the Ethiopian rescued Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:7-13). The Queen of Sheba visited Solomon.

In the New Testament, Simon of Cyrene carried Jesus' cross; people from Egypt and Libya heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:10); the Ethiopian treasurer believed and was baptized (Acts 8:26-39); and Africans led the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1).

"Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God" (Psalm 68:31).

lessons.title: North Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia
lessons.body:
By AD 200 North Africa was a strong centre of Christianity, producing Tertullian, Cyprian and later Augustine. Alexandria in Egypt had a famous Christian school and great leaders like Athanasius. Egypt also gave birth to monasticism through Antony.

In the fourth century the kingdom of Aksum in **Ethiopia** became Christian under King Ezana through Frumentius. The **Ethiopian Orthodox Church** has continued for over 1,600 years, with its own Bible translation and traditions. The **Coptic Church** of Egypt has survived centuries as a minority. Christian kingdoms also flourished in Nubia (modern Sudan) for centuries.

lessons.title: Decline and early European contact
lessons.body:
From the seventh century the spread of Islam across North Africa led to the decline of the church there. Divisions, a faith held mainly by the elite, and a Bible not translated into local Berber languages may have weakened it. The lesson: a church needs Scripture in the heart language and deep discipleship.

From the fifteenth century Portuguese explorers brought Catholic missionaries. The kingdom of **Kongo** had a Christian king, Afonso I (early 1500s). There were also Catholic contacts with the kingdoms of **Benin** and **Warri** in what is now Nigeria. But these early efforts were entangled with the slave trade and had limited lasting effect.

modules.title: The Gospel Comes to Nigeria
modules.intro: In the nineteenth century the gospel spread across Nigeria through missionaries and African believers. This week we trace that story.

lessons.title: Badagry, Abeokuta and the Yoruba
lessons.body:
Freed slaves, many of Yoruba origin, became Christians in Sierra Leone. Some returned home and asked for missionaries.

In **1842** Methodist missionary **Thomas Birch Freeman** arrived at **Badagry**, followed by **Henry Townsend** of the Church Missionary Society (CMS). Missions spread to **Abeokuta**, where Egba rulers welcomed them, and then to Ibadan, Ogbomoso and Lagos.

**Samuel Ajayi Crowther**, captured as a boy and rescued from a slave ship, became a teacher, linguist and priest. He led the translation of the Bible into Yoruba and in **1864** was consecrated the first African Anglican bishop, leading the Niger Mission.

lessons.title: The East, the Niger and Calabar
lessons.body:
Presbyterian missionaries from Jamaica and Scotland arrived in **Calabar** in **1846**, led by Hope Waddell. **Mary Slessor** served from 1876 for nearly forty years, living among the people, rescuing twins who would otherwise be killed, and opposing other cruel practices.

Crowther's Niger Mission, staffed largely by African agents, planted churches along the River Niger at Onitsha and elsewhere.

Roman Catholic missions (the Society of African Missions from the 1860s, and the Holy Ghost Fathers in the east) also grew strongly, building many schools. Today Catholics and Anglicans are especially numerous in the south-east.

lessons.title: The North and the Middle Belt
lessons.body:
Northern Nigeria, largely Muslim, was harder to reach. In **1893** Walter Gowans, Thomas Kent and Rowland Bingham set out for the interior; Gowans and Kent died, but Bingham persevered and the **Sudan Interior Mission** (SIM) was established. Its churches became the **Evangelical Church Winning All** (ECWA).

The Sudan United Mission and others worked in the Middle Belt, where many peoples turned to Christ. Churches such as COCIN (Church of Christ in Nations) grew from this work.

Missionaries and African evangelists paid a great price: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit" (John 12:24).

modules.title: African-Led Christianity
modules.intro: Africans have led the church's growth on the continent. This week we study African-initiated churches, African theologians and missions.

lessons.title: African-initiated churches
lessons.body:
From the 1880s some Africans formed churches independent of mission control, often because of racism or a desire for African leadership and worship. In Lagos, the **Native Baptist Church** (1888) and the **United Native African Church** (1891) were early examples.

In the twentieth century the **Aladura** churches emphasised prayer, healing, dreams and visions, and the 1930 revival under Joseph Babalola led to the Christ Apostolic Church.

These churches showed that Africans could lead and express the faith in African ways. Some, however, mixed Christianity with traditional practices. Each must be tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11).

lessons.title: African theologians and leaders
lessons.body:
African Christians have contributed much to theology:

- **Byang Kato** (1936-1975), a Nigerian ECWA leader, warned against universalism and syncretism in *Theological Pitfalls in Africa* and called for theology both African and biblical.
- **Kwame Bediako** (Ghana) and **John Mbiti** (Kenya) explored how the gospel relates to African culture and religion.
- **Tokunboh Adeyemo** (Nigeria) led the Association of Evangelicals in Africa and edited the *Africa Bible Commentary* (2006), written by African scholars.

African theology asks: how does the unchanging gospel speak to African questions of ancestors, spirits, community, power and suffering?

lessons.title: Nigeria as a sending nation
lessons.body:
Nigeria has become a missionary-sending nation. **Calvary Ministries (CAPRO)**, founded in 1975 by Nigerian graduates, sends missionaries to unreached peoples in Nigeria and beyond. The ECWA Evangelical Missionary Society, the Nigerian Baptist Convention and many Pentecostal churches send missionaries across Africa and the world.

Nigerian churches have also planted congregations among the diaspora in Europe and America.

Yet many peoples within Nigeria remain unreached, especially in the north. The task given in Acts 1:8 is not finished: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria are near at hand.

modules.title: Challenges and Calling Today
modules.intro: The Nigerian church is large and vibrant but faces serious challenges. This week we study them and the church's calling.

lessons.title: Syncretism and the spirit world
lessons.body:
**Syncretism** mixes Christian faith with other religious practices: consulting diviners, wearing charms, offering to ancestors, or treating Christian objects as magic. Israel did the same: "They feared the LORD, and served their own gods" (2 Kings 17:33).

African Christians rightly take the spirit world seriously, as the Bible does (Ephesians 6:12). The answer is not denial but Christ's supremacy: He "spoiled principalities and powers" (Colossians 2:15) and is the only Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).

The church must teach clearly, disciple deeply and provide biblical answers to people's fears about witchcraft, sickness and the future.

lessons.title: Prosperity, division and shallow discipleship
lessons.body:
Other challenges include:

- **Prosperity teaching** that makes wealth the measure of faith and leads to exploitation (1 Timothy 6:5-10).
- **Division**: countless splits over leadership and money (1 Corinthians 1:10-13).
- **Shallow discipleship**: large crowds but weak Bible knowledge and little change in society. Nigeria has many churches yet struggles with corruption and injustice.
- **Unaccountable leadership**: leaders above correction (1 Peter 5:2-3).

The remedy is faithful preaching of the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), discipleship that changes lives (Matthew 28:20), and leaders who serve humbly.

lessons.title: Persecution and hope
lessons.body:
Christians in parts of northern Nigeria and the Middle Belt have suffered violent attacks, kidnappings and the destruction of churches and villages. Many have died for their faith. The church must pray, care for victims and displaced families, speak for justice, and refuse revenge (Romans 12:19-21; Hebrews 13:3).

Despite challenges, there is great hope. The gospel has transformed millions of Nigerians. The church can be salt and light in politics, business, education and media, and send missionaries to the nations.

The vision is the throne room of Revelation 7:9: people "of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues", including every Nigerian people, praising the Lamb.

assignments.title: The gospel in my people group
assignments.prompt: Research and write how the gospel first came to your town, people group or region in Nigeria (or another African country). Name the people involved, the challenges they faced and the state of the church there today.

assignments.title: Answering syncretism
assignments.prompt: Describe a common form of syncretism in your community. Using Scripture from this course, explain why it is wrong and how the church can help believers trust Christ fully in the face of fear of spirits, sickness or misfortune.
